title: We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together
description: A one-take whirlwind through a pop-up-book apartment, with Swift changing outfits on the run while her band performs in animal costumes.

pops.text: Lead single from Red, and Swift's first team-up single with Swedish hitmakers Max Martin and Shellback — the start of her full pop pivot.
Origin story: a friend of an ex walked into the studio saying the couple were getting back together. Swift's flat denial became the hook, and the song came together in about 25 minutes.
That spoken bridge — 'like, ever' — was kept deliberately conversational, as if she is venting to friends mid-song rather than singing at you.
Chart rocket: it debuted at No. 72 on the Hot 100 off just two days of airplay, then leapt straight to No. 1 the next week.
It was her first-ever Hot 100 No. 1, and it held the top spot for three non-consecutive weeks.
First-week digital sales topped 620,000 copies — at the time a record-setting debut week for a female artist.
Director Declan Whitebloom shot the video in one continuous take, with five costume looks swapped behind walls while the camera kept moving.
Spot the band: her backing musicians perform in full woodland-animal costumes for no explained reason — pure breakup delirium.
Rolling Stone named it the second-best song of 2012, and it earned a Grammy nomination for Record of the Year.

title: I Knew You Were Trouble
description: A gritty desert-and-rave mini-movie in which Swift, pink-tipped hair and all, looks back on a toxic romance she walked into with eyes open.

pops.text: Swift has said the song should sound as chaotic as the feeling that inspired it — falling for someone after seeing every red flag.
Co-written and produced with Max Martin and Shellback, it was built around electric guitars and synths before the bass drops hit.
That wobbling dubstep refrain was a radical break from her country-pop sound in 2012 — critics were split, fans were not.
It debuted at No. 3 on the Hot 100 with about 416,000 downloads, making Swift the first artist with two songs debuting at 400,000-plus.
Peaked at No. 2 on the Hot 100, held off the top by Bruno Mars, but it ruled Billboard's Pop Songs chart for seven weeks.
Director Anthony Mandler opens the video with a spoken monologue before any music — a short-film framing unusual for her videos then.
Broadway's Reeve Carney plays the trouble in question, opposite Swift in desert, motel and rave scenes shot around Los Angeles.
The video premiered on December 13, 2012 — Swift's 23rd birthday.
Its pop-radio success helped convince Swift to go all-in on pop for her next album, 1989.

description: Swift and her real-life best friends bounce on trampolines, hit the Malibu beach and throw a house party in a square 4:3 frame.

pops.text: Swift called being 22 her favorite year yet — old enough to plan a life, young enough to know you know almost nothing.
Another Max Martin and Shellback collaboration from Red, released as the album's fourth single in March 2013.
The video is presented in a boxy 4:3 aspect ratio, giving the whole day-out a home-movie feel.
Director Anthony Mandler shot it in Malibu in February 2013, including beach scenes and a shopping-cart ride.
No actors as pals: Swift insisted the friends in the video are her actual best friends, and said she forgot it was a shoot.
Actress Jessica Szohr is among the friends making a cameo in the party scenes.
The video premiered March 13, 2013 — the 13th being Swift's lucky number — the same day the Red Tour opened.
That white tee reading 'Not A Lot Going On At The Moment' became so iconic she recreated the look on the Eras Tour.
A limited, individually numbered CD single was sold through her store alongside Red Tour gear.

title: Style
description: An abstract, double-exposed reverie of Swift and Dominic Sherwood in woods, beaches and headlights — no plot, all mood.

pops.text: Third single from 1989, written with Max Martin, Shellback and Ali Payami, built on a sleek electric-guitar riff and pulsing synths.
The sound blends pop with funk and disco touches — a long way from the banjos of her early records.
Lyrically it flips her older right-versus-wrong breakup songs: here both lovers keep circling back, and neither is blameless.
It peaked at No. 6 on the Hot 100, giving 1989 its third consecutive top-10 single.
The single was later certified triple platinum in the United States.
Director Kyle Newman premiered the video on February 13, 2015 — a Friday the 13th, fitting Swift's lucky number.
Dominic Sherwood co-stars; his mismatched eye colors — one blue, one part-brown — became a fan talking point overnight.
Shot around Los Angeles, the video layers the lovers' faces over beaches, forests and smoke instead of telling a straight story.
Newman wove in pieces of Swift's own personal footage, making the abstract clip feel oddly intimate.

title: Wildest Dreams
description: A 1950s movie-within-a-video: brunette Swift plays an actress falling for co-star Scott Eastwood on an African film set, then loses him at the premiere.

pops.text: Listen to the pulse under the song: it is built around a recording of Swift's own resting heartbeat.
Co-written and produced with Max Martin and Shellback, it is 1989's dream-pop ballad — a plea to be remembered even if the love fails.
It became 1989's fifth consecutive top-10 single, peaking at No. 5 on the Hot 100 and topping Billboard's Radio Songs chart.
Director Joseph Kahn — of 'Blank Space' and 'Bad Blood' — premiered the video during the 2015 MTV VMAs pre-show.
Scott Eastwood later said his agents called the video a bad idea; Swift phoned him personally, and he did it anyway.
Swift's character is named Marjorie Finn, a nod to her grandmother Marjorie Finlay; Eastwood plays Robert Kingsley.
Kahn modeled the romance on Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton and classics like The African Queen and Out of Africa.
Giraffes, zebras and a lion wander the set — Swift donated all her proceeds from the video to the African Parks Foundation of America.
A remix by Dutch DJ R3hab followed in October 2015, giving the hushed ballad a dance-floor second life.

title: Out of the Woods
description: Taylor battles forests, snow, wolves and fire in New Zealand landscapes, crawling through mud in a blue dress until she finally finds herself on a beach.

pops.text: First released in October 2014 as a promotional preview of 1989, this did not become a full single until early 2016 — a slow-burn rollout for a fan favorite.
Taylor co-wrote and co-produced it with Jack Antonoff. He built the pulsing synth track first and sent it to her while she was on a plane.
She wrote the melody and lyrics in about 30 minutes on that flight. The anxious, repeating chorus was designed to feel like a relationship that never quite settles.
Antonoff layered in his own background vocals and heavy, looping drums. The result mixes synth-pop with a darker, almost chant-like intensity.
The song peaked at No. 18 on the Billboard Hot 100, and reached the top 10 in Canada and New Zealand. It later earned platinum certification in the US.
Director Joseph Kahn premiered the video on Dick Clark's New Year's Rockin' Eve on December 31, 2015. No male lead — the story is Taylor versus the elements alone.
Kahn said Taylor did her own stunts with no double, staying in the mud for hours and lying in real snow in a sleeveless dress to keep the shoot moving.
It was filmed in New Zealand, including Bethells Beach near Auckland. That same blue dress reappears on zombie Taylor at the start of 'Look What You Made Me Do.'
Taylor later re-recorded it as 'Out of the Woods (Taylor's Version)' for 1989 (Taylor's Version) in 2023, reclaiming the song she had previewed almost a decade earlier.

title: ...Ready For It?
description: A hooded Taylor confronts a cyborg version of herself trapped in a glass box in a neon sci-fi world riffing on Tron, Blade Runner and Ghost in the Shell.

pops.text: Taylor first teased this during an ESPN college football broadcast on September 2, 2017, then dropped it for download the very next day.
She wrote it with producers Max Martin, Shellback and Ali Payami. It opens Reputation as a deliberate shock: heavy synths, bass drops and programmed drums.
Yes, that is Taylor rapping in the verses — a first for her as a lead artist. The sweet, soaring chorus then flips the tough criminal imagery into pure infatuation.
It debuted and peaked at No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100, her 22nd top-10 hit at the time, and topped the Digital Songs chart with 135,000 first-week downloads.
Director Joseph Kahn shot the video on August 21, 2017, weeks before anyone had heard the full album. It premiered October 26 and drew about 20.4 million views in its first day.
Spot the graffiti early on: '89' and '91' — Taylor's birth year and Joe Alwyn's. Walls also hide phrases like 'UR Gorgeous' and 'I Love You In Secret.'
The cyborg in the bodysuit is not a villain from outside — it is Taylor herself. She shatters the glass with her voice, destroying the hooded Taylor in the process.
Kahn loaded the clip with sci-fi and anime nods, from a light-cycle-style ride to that white horse, all shot in a rain-slick, Blade Runner-style city set.
It was certified double platinum in the US in July 2018. On the Reputation Stadium Tour it opened the show — the question in the title became the night's kickoff.

title: End Game
description: Taylor parties across Miami, Tokyo and London with Ed Sheeran and Future — yachts, karaoke, arcade games, a double-decker bus and a late-night kebab shop.

pops.text: This is the only track on Reputation with featured guests — and it stacks two at once: longtime friend Ed Sheeran and rapper Future, Taylor's first collaboration with him.
Produced by Max Martin and Shellback, who also co-wrote it with all three performers. Ed later said he wrote his verse thinking about meeting his now-wife Cherry at Taylor's house.
Released as Reputation's third single, it peaked at No. 18 on the Billboard Hot 100 and No. 11 in Canada, and hit No. 10 on US Pop Airplay.
Director Joseph Kahn filmed in three cities: Miami, Tokyo and London. Taylor dances with Future on a yacht in Miami and does karaoke and arcade games in Tokyo.
To stop leaks, the London pub dancers heard no song at all — only a click track in the room, while Taylor sang along to the real track through hidden earbuds.
Eagle eyes: Taylor plays a snake video game in a hotel room, reclaiming the snake insult thrown at her, and wears snakeskin while riding a motorcycle.
Her lucky 13 turns up on the car she rides in with Future. In Tokyo, neon signs flash lyrics like 'big reputation,' plus her cats' names, Meredith and Olivia.
The London ending is deliberately ordinary: shots with Ed, a red bus, the Millennium Bridge, and a stop at Kentish Delight, a real Kentish Town kebab shop.
The video premiered January 12, 2018 after a Good Morning America tease. It was the third Reputation video in a row directed by Kahn.

title: Lover
description: Inside a snow globe, Taylor and dancer Christian Owens live out a whole relationship in a colorful dollhouse where each room holds a different chapter — and album.

pops.text: Taylor wrote this one entirely alone, late at night at the piano in her Nashville home. She said she wanted a timeless love song that could play at a wedding reception.
She sent Jack Antonoff a voice memo, and the next day at Electric Lady Studios in New York they finished it in about six hours with engineer Laura Sisk.
Antonoff said Taylor 'wrote every stitch' before she arrived. The recording used only older instruments — live drums, upright piano, Mellotron and a Paul McCartney-inspired bassline.
It is a slow waltz, not a four-on-the-floor pop song. Taylor imagined it as the last two people on a dance floor swaying at three in the morning.
Released August 16, 2019, a week before the album, it peaked at No. 10 on the Billboard Hot 100 and became a perennial wedding and first-dance favorite.
Taylor co-directed the video with Drew Kirsch; it premiered August 22, 2019, hours before the Lover album arrived. The male lead is Christian Owens, a dancer from her 1989 and Reputation tours.
The concept came from her own lyric in 'You Are in Love' about dancing in a snow globe. The dollhouse inside has seven distinctly colored rooms, one echoing each album up to Lover.
Look for the blue room's giant fishbowl the couple swim in, board games in the yellow room, and home movies in the attic. Critics compared the pastel look to Wes Anderson films.
The final reveal: the little girl given the snow globe at Christmas is the couple's daughter. A Shawn Mendes duet remix followed in November 2019, with verses he wrote himself.

title: Bejeweled
description: Taylor's self-directed Cinderella twist: scrubbing floors for Laura Dern and the Haim sisters, then winning a talent contest, dancing in martini glasses with Dita Von Teese, and ghosting the prince.

pops.text: From Midnights, Taylor's tenth album, released October 21, 2022. She co-wrote 'Bejeweled' with Jack Antonoff, who also co-produced the shimmering synth track.
In its first week Taylor became the first artist ever to hold the entire Billboard Hot 100 top 10 with one album — 'Bejeweled' sat at No. 6 in that clean sweep.
Taylor wrote and directed the video herself; it premiered October 25, 2022 — exactly 12 years to the day after her album Speak Now was released, a date fans did not think was an accident.
The casting is stacked: Laura Dern plays the wicked stepmother, the three Haim sisters are the stepsisters, and makeup legend Pat McGrath appears as a queen.
Burlesque star Dita Von Teese plays the Fairy Goddess, and the two perform a matching routine in giant martini glasses — Von Teese taught Taylor her signature moves for it.
Instead of losing a glass slipper, this Cinderella enters a talent contest to win her castle. When Prince Jack — played by Antonoff — proposes at the end, title cards say she ghosted him.
Fans counted elevator buttons and costume changes pointing to Speak Now: purple dresses, dragon imagery echoing 'Long Live,' and a 'Speak Now' orchestral snippet in the outro.
Those clues were right — Speak Now (Taylor's Version) was indeed her next re-recording, announced in May 2023 and released that July.
Taylor told fans the video was made 'specifically for you' and packed with Easter eggs. It became a fixture of the Eras Tour, complete with the viral 'Bejeweled' strut dance.

title: Lavender Haze
description: The dreamy Midnights opener gets a self-directed, purple-soaked video that Swift called a sultry sleepless 70s fever dream.

pops.text: Pop-up! Swift found the phrase 'lavender haze' while watching Mad Men — it was 1950s slang for that all-encompassing glow of being in love.
This is track one on Midnights, the opener that sets the whole sleepless, after-midnight mood for the album.
Check the credits: actor Zoë Kravitz is a co-writer here, alongside Jack Antonoff and Kendrick Lamar producer Sounwave.
It debuted at No. 2 on the Hot 100 — in the week Swift became the first artist ever to hold the entire top 10 at once.
Radio loved it too: the song became Swift's record-tying 27th top 10 on Billboard's Adult Pop Airplay chart.
Swift wrote and directed this video herself — it was the first of the Midnights videos for which she wrote the treatment.
Her love interest is played by Laith Ashley, a model and transgender activist Swift said she adored working with.
That torn-open TV spilling out a cosmic aquarium of giant koi fish? Pure fever dream — the whole clip swims in purple and 1970s decor.
Under the haze, the lyric is a shield: Swift wrote it about tuning out tabloid noise to protect a real relationship.

title: Fortnight
description: The lead single from The Tortured Poets Department, featuring Post Malone — a black-and-white tale of a two-week romance that ruins everything beautifully.

pops.text: Pop-up! A fortnight is British for two weeks — and this whole song is a whirlwind romance that burns out in exactly that span.
Post Malone co-wrote the song and takes the second verse. Swift said his melodies 'stick in your head forever.'
On release day, April 19, 2024, this became Spotify's most-streamed song in a single day — ever, at that point.
It debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, becoming Swift's 12th career chart-topper.
Swift directed the video herself and shot it in stark black and white, opening on her chained to a bed in an upside-down room.
Those stern scientists experimenting on Swift? That's Ethan Hawke and Josh Charles — stars of Dead Poets Society, a wink at the album's title.
When Swift wipes her face in the video, Post Malone's famous face tattoos appear on her skin instead.
At the typewriters, both stars hammer out the song's most-quoted line: 'I love you, it's ruining my life.'
The video dropped the evening of April 19, 2024 — just hours after the album arrived, and hours before its surprise Anthology expansion.

title: Wilson
description: Audio only — no official music video exists. This is the celebrated A Live One recording of the Gamehendge villain's theme, captured at Phish's Madison Square Garden debut on December 30, 1994.

pops.text: Pop-up! Wilson is the villain of Gamehendge, Phish's mythical land — he's the King of Prussia and Duke of Lizards, and this song is a taunt aimed straight at him.
Wilson was the first Phish song to mention Gamehendge by name, arriving way back in 1986.
It grew out of a narrative poem by lyricist Tom Marshall and band friend Aaron Woolf — Woolf still gets a writing credit.
The Gamehendge songs formed Trey Anastasio's senior project at Goddard College, The Man Who Stepped Into Yesterday.
Hear that crowd roar? The famous 'Wilson!' chant was first documented on April 15, 1994, at New York's Beacon Theatre.
This very recording opened Phish's first-ever show at Madison Square Garden, on December 30, 1994.
A Live One, the album built around performances like this, became Phish's first gold-certified release.
The song's parting shot is a mocking question to the king: 'Wilson, can you still have fun?'
This A Live One version of Wilson later turned up as a playable track in the Rock Band video game series.

title: Tweezer
description: Phish's mightiest jam vehicle, caught live on the legendary 1998 Island Tour in Providence — the composed song is just the launchpad for the improvisation to come.

pops.text: Pop-up! Tweezer debuted on March 28, 1990, at a frat-house party at Denison University — the same night Cavern and Runaway Jim were first played.
All four band members share the writing credit, which fits: live, Tweezer belongs to whoever grabs the jam first.
The studio version anchors A Picture of Nectar (1992), Phish's major-label debut, named for Nectar Rorris of the Burlington bar where the band started out.
The lyric is gloriously silly: step into the freezer and meet Uncle Ebenezer, who's apparently already in there.
The album doesn't let it go — a short, rowdy Tweezer Reprise returns to close the record.
For A Live One, Phish included a Bangor, Maine Tweezer that runs 30 minutes and 55 seconds — on an official album!
The longest known Tweezer, from Memphis in 1995, stretched to just under 50 minutes of improvisation.
The 2013 Tahoe Tweezer — 36 minutes of soaring peaks — is still name-checked by fans as an all-time great jam.
By the song's 30th birthday in 2020, Phish had played it more than 410 times — roughly once every four shows.

title: Run Like an Antelope
description: Audio only — official live audio provided by JEMP Records from The Gorge '98, with no music video. One of Phish's oldest songs and a signature set-closing sprint.

pops.text: Pop-up! Antelope predates Phish itself — an early version sits on Trey Anastasio's 1983 demo tape Bivouac Jaun.
The name tips a hat to Space Antelope, one of the bands Trey played in at boarding school.
On that first demo, Trey reportedly played all the instruments himself, while Tom Marshall and the Dude of Life supplied the words.
The demo version also landed on the Phish White Tape that the band sold and handed out in its earliest days.
Listen for the gleeful nonsense shout 'Rye, Rye, Rocco!' — live, that line gets bent into new variations whenever Trey is feeling it.
Another name gets swapped around live: Marco Esquandolas has been replaced mid-show by everyone from band crew to, once, Guyute.
Antelope became one of the most dependable first-set closers in Phish history — the signal to sprint to the set break.
At the 1996 Clifford Ball festival, the band jammed Antelope while acrobats performed around them.
This recording comes from The Gorge in 1998 and was released to YouTube by JEMP Records, the band's own label.

title: The Lizards
description: Official audio only — no official music video exists. The linchpin of Trey Anastasio's Gamehendge saga, introducing Colonel Forbin to the Lizards, King Wilson, and the Helping Friendly Book.

pops.text: Welcome to Gamehendge! This song is the linchpin of the whole saga — nearly every stray Phish character and plot thread was pulled together inside 'The Lizards.'
Trey Anastasio built the song for his senior thesis at Goddard College, a full musical called The Man Who Stepped Into Yesterday.
Meet Colonel Forbin, the retired colonel who walks through a door in the woods and steps straight into the land of Gamehendge.
His guide is Rutherford the Brave, a knight who explains how the gentle Lizards lost their sacred Helping Friendly Book to the evil King Wilson.
Rutherford gets so fired up retelling the story that he leaps into a river — forgetting he is wearing full metal armor — and promptly sinks.
He is rescued just in time by Tela and the Unit-Monster, one of Gamehendge's strangest and most beloved rescues.
The Helping Friendly Book was written by Icculus, the Lizards' god, and supposedly holds the secrets of eternal joy. Wilson keeps it locked away to keep the Lizards under his thumb.
The song's most quoted line became a Phish life motto: 'The trick was to surrender to the flow.'
Debuted live in 1988, 'The Lizards' was an anchor of nearly every show through the mid-1990s before becoming a once-a-tour treat.
Phish staged the complete Gamehendge cycle only a handful of times over the decades, which makes every full 'Lizards' feel like opening a storybook.

title: Maze
description: Official audio only — the studio version from Rift (1993), Phish's claustrophobic concept album. A frenetic Page-and-Trey showcase built on pure musical tension.

pops.text: Official audio: this is the studio cut from Rift, Phish's 1993 concept album tracing a relationship coming apart, produced by Barry Beckett in Nashville.
'Maze' debuted live on the spring 1992 tour and instantly became a crowd favorite for its frenetic pace and full-throttle energy.
The lyric is a panic attack in song form — a narrator convinced he will never find his way out, no matter which way he turns.
Page McConnell absolutely pounds the piano and organ here. 'Maze' became one of his signature spotlight songs in concert.
Listen for the family resemblance: the openings of 'Maze' and 'David Bowie' are so similar that Phish once started one on 11/4/98 and played the other, just to mess with the crowd.
In 1994 Trey began weaving his digital delay loop into the jam, giving 'Maze' a dizzy, spiraling second gear on stage.
Early versions were tight, first-set Type I rockers. By the mid-90s the song had grown into a genuine second-set jam vehicle.
The 10/18/96 Pittsburgh version is still name-checked by fans as a heavyweight-champion 'Maze' that broke far outside the song's usual walls.
True to its title, the composed sections keep doubling back on themselves — every apparent exit drops you into another corridor of riffs.

title: Stash
description: Official live video from Phish's own channel: New Year's Eve 1993 at the Worcester Centrum, the band's biggest headlining show to that point. Phish's ultimate tension-and-release workout, from A Picture of Nectar.

pops.text: This performance is from New Year's Eve 1993 in Worcester — Phish's first show at the 14,800-capacity Centrum and the start of their elaborate New Year's Eve gag tradition, aquarium set and all.
Trey wrote 'Stash' in early 1990 while deep in a jazz phase, soaking up Benny Goodman with Charlie Christian, Miles Davis, Coltrane, and Charles Mingus.
The whole song is a masterclass in tension and release — a music-theory idea Trey was studying, built on the classic jazz ii-V-I pull back home.
Lyrics are by Tom Marshall, Trey's childhood friend and longtime writing partner, wrapped around a smuggler's tale of a stash that has to be hidden.
'Stash' landed on A Picture of Nectar in 1992, Phish's major-label debut for Elektra, dedicated to Nectar Rorris of the Burlington bar where the band learned to play.
Fans turned the song's sharp composed accents into an audience participation ritual — listen for the crowd clapping along with the band's hits.
No two versions peak the same way. The jam just keeps tightening the screws, which is why fans trade favorite 'Stashes' like vintage wine years.
The fall 1995 Orlando 'Stash' famously detoured through Dizzy Gillespie's 'Manteca' and 'Dog Faced Boy' without ever fully leaving the song behind.
'Stash' later reached a whole new audience as downloadable content for the video game Rock Band 3.

title: Fee
description: Official audio only — the opening track of Junta (1989), Phish's debut album. A jaunty, surreal love story about Fee the weasel and Floyd the chimpanzee.

pops.text: Official audio: 'Fee' opens Junta, Phish's self-produced debut, recorded at Euphoria Sound Studios in Revere, Massachusetts and first self-released on cassette in May 1989.
The band produced Junta themselves and, because the studio had no mix automation, gathered around the console to perform the fades together by hand.
It is a love story, Phish-style: Fee is a weasel, Floyd is a chimpanzee, and their romance survives a villain named Millie and a very well-timed rescue.
That bizarre nipple paper-cut lyric is a running gag — the same image turns up in 'Punch You in the Eye' and 'The Sloth.' Only in Gamehendge, folks.
For many early-90s fans, this jaunty story-song — not the big prog workouts — was the first Phish track that hooked them for good.
Phish's first label liked it so much that 'Fee' was added as a bonus track to the first CD pressing of the next album, Lawn Boy.
Live, Trey traditionally sings the verses through a megaphone, a gloriously lo-fi touch the band still breaks out decades later — including at Sphere.
Junta is pronounced 'hoon-tah' and was named after Ben 'Junta' Hunter, the band's first official manager.
The album was later certified Gold after Elektra reissued it in 1992 — not bad for a cassette the band used to sell at shows.

title: Harry Hood
description: Official live video from Phish's own channel: New Year's Eve 1993 at the Worcester Centrum, a version Phish.net counts among the strongest of a transformative year. You can feel good about Hood!

pops.text: This is 12/31/93 in Worcester, one of four standout 'Harry Hoods' from 1993 — and this show launched Phish's New Year's Eve spectacle tradition with an aquarium set and a giant clam.
Harry Hood was a real guy — sort of. He was the smiling milkman mascot of the Hood dairy company, whose bottling plant sat directly across from the band's house on King Street in Burlington.
The plant's giant milk tanks bore Harry's grinning face, lit up at night. Housemate Brian Long asked the question that built the song: 'Harry, where do you go when the lights go out?'
The other half of the lyric came from the mail. A former tenant, Mr. A. Miner, kept getting form letters cheerfully thanking him — hence 'Thank you, Mr. Miner.'
Trey drafted parts of the music after a wild summer 1985 trip to Greece with Jon Fishman that involved a sea storm and a capsized raft.
'Harry Hood' debuted live on 10/30/85 at Hunt's in Burlington, making it one of the oldest songs still anchoring Phish shows.
The beloved 4/18/92 version pays extended homage to Vince Guaraldi's Peanuts music — fans simply call it the 'Linus and Lucy' Hood.
At Red Rocks on 8/6/96 the crowd started answering the band's 'Harry!' with a shouted 'Hood!' — an audience ritual that has stuck ever since.
One week later at The Great Went in 1997, fans filled the air with flying glowsticks during 'Hood' until it looked like the Northern Lights — and a Phish tradition was born.
In 1998 Neil Young joined an acoustic 'Harry Hood' at the Bridge School Benefit, then stuck around to sing his own 'Helpless' with the band.
